intro: Everything still open for you is on this page, each question with its evidence on the same screen. Answer in the chat, by the question's letter or by its title. Each question stands alone: answer any of them, in any order, and leave the rest for later.

Three tags say where a question stands. Open: no answer yet. Applied, please confirm: the change is already in the promise's wording, and one word from you keeps it or undoes it. Recommendation changed by the earlier candidate: drawing the earlier candidate (the shape of the engine's parts drawn from today's engine, now one input among the panel's) changed what we recommend, and the [[page:changes]] has the earlier recommendation.

Under each question, "What we know" lists the facts the answer rests on: the requirements, the decisions already made, the earlier candidate, and today's engine, which is evidence and never the reason for a design. Most facts link to the promise, quality target, extension case, decision, part or design flaw they come from, so you can read more before you answer.

The letters are new in this version. The withdrawn question on how much the test rig proves before design, the earlier letters and numbers, and every earlier wording live in the [[page:changes]]. Only the list at the end, Decided, records what you have decided.

questions.title: Do the quality targets say how well the engine must work?
questions.decides: Whether the quality targets on [[page:requirements]], grouped under twelve qualities, are the measure the panel and the design rounds design against, and which of the numbers they leave open you set now.
evidence: A quality is something every part of the engine must have so that a promise holds everywhere, not in one place. Each target tells a situation at a show, in rehearsal, at the desk or in development, so that it can be tested: what happens, then what must be true. The targets say what is needed, never how to build it.

There are forty-two targets under twelve qualities: staying up through a live show; every screen telling the truth; the designer's iteration speed; operating it without technical help; easy to understand and change, for people and for AI agents; easy to extend; testable without the live show; privacy and access; running well on the show machine and the venue network at the size of a show; standalone and offline; safe release and rollback; and more than one copy, kit or pack without rework.
Each target names the promises it serves, and every promise is served by at least four targets.

Most targets rest on a decision you have already made or a roadmap section you ratified. Three are proposed in full, [[qt:QT3]], [[qt:QT5]] and [[qt:QT17]]: they rest on the pass's questions and on the promises' test situations, which you have not ruled on one by one. Five are proposed in part: [[qt:QT13]] (that building the machine itself needs no terminal), [[qt:QT19]] (a page per piece of the engine, and the newcomer measure), [[qt:QT31]] (the automatic check for a committed secret), [[qt:QT33]] (the sizes and limits, and a preflight that refuses a start over a load limit) and [[qt:QT34]] (that the profile declares the number of phones and the preflight counts them).

Two targets wait on questions on this page: [[qt:QT37]] on [[q:M]], and [[qt:QT39]] on [[q:L]], [[q:M]] and [[q:N]]. The other open point of [[qt:QT37]], where the standalone fact is kept, belongs to the design rounds. [[qt:QT3]] leaves what a disconnected tablet does with a scan to the design round on where authority lives across devices.
The panel gets the confirmed targets in its brief, beside the promises and the extension cases, and runs only after you confirm them ([[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]]).
Fourteen targets leave a number for you to set. They follow, one per line.
[[qt:QT1]]: how long the engine may take from power back to a running show.
[[qt:QT2]]: how many restarts the program watcher tries, and over how long, before it shows red; and to confirm ten seconds for the controls to come back, from the promise's test situation.
[[qt:QT3]]: to confirm five seconds for a tablet to be back under its own station name, from the promise's test situation.
[[qt:QT5]]: how long after the engine goes silent a screen must say so (today, the scanners' polling interval).
[[qt:QT9]]: the minutes from publish to playing, the promise's "within minutes".
[[qt:QT13]]: how long the venue technician may need from an unpacked kit to a go.
[[qt:QT14]]: how long from power on to a running show.
[[qt:QT19]]: how long a newcomer may need to make and prove a first small change.
[[qt:QT30]]: how long each kind of data is kept by default, per game.

[[qt:QT33]]: the kit size to design for, within a few dozen devices (tablets, scanners, screens, speakers); the time a scan is answered in; the time a live message takes to reach every tablet; the machine's limits for load, memory, disk and temperature; and to confirm half a second for a video to report started, from the promise's test situation.
[[qt:QT34]]: the number of player phones one kit carries.
[[qt:QT35]]: the longest acceptable first sync for a hardware scanner (today 5 to 15 minutes for 30 to 40 MB).
[[qt:QT40]]: how many scans a device must be able to keep while offline.
[[qt:QT43]]: how many copies of the engine one machine must carry at once.

options.label: Confirm the targets as the base and set the numbers now.
options.cost: Fourteen numbers to settle at once; a number set before anything is measured may need resetting once the build half's first version runs.

options.label: Confirm the targets and leave the numbers to the design rounds.
options.cost: The panel designs without them; a target without its number is harder to test, and each number comes back to you as a question in the round that uses it.

questions.recommendation: Confirm the forty-two as the base. Set now the numbers you already know from running the show (how long a boot or a restart may take, the kit size, how long records are kept); for the rest, say that the panel may propose a number and you will confirm it in the design round that uses it. A target you do not want changes the brief the panel gets, so name it now.

questions.title: Do the extension cases say how the engine must grow?
questions.decides: Whether the twenty-four extension cases on [[page:requirements]] are the ways the platform must grow that the panel and the design rounds design for, and whether any way of growing you plan is missing.
evidence: Each case tells who grows the platform, what they should need to touch, what must stay untouched, and when it is due: a designer making a whole second game ([[ex:EX1]]), a designer adding a third thing a team can do with a token ([[ex:EX3]]), a venue technician fitting the kit to a new room ([[ex:EX13]]), an operator with a second kit ([[ex:EX16]]), a director telling the night from the record ([[ex:EX19]]), a developer from outside the team ([[ex:EX21]]).

The cases say what is needed, never how to build it. Every case rests on a decision you have made or a roadmap section you ratified, except [[ex:EX15]], a new lighting system or video player, whose need rests on the room promise and the glossary and whose how (how the engine reaches its programs, and where the start-or-use setting lives) waits for the design rounds.
Each case names the promises it serves, and every promise is served by at least three cases.

Two cases carry a number for you to set: [[ex:EX10]], how many phones one kit carries at once, which is the same number as [[qt:QT34]]; and [[ex:EX12]], how many GM tablets one standalone game may run, which [[q:M]] decides.

Three cases name choices kept for the design rounds, listed under Coming in the design rounds below: where the standalone declaration lives ([[ex:EX12]]), where the designer's trial copy of the engine runs ([[ex:EX14]]) and where the start-or-use setting lives ([[ex:EX15]]).
The panel gets the confirmed cases in its brief, beside the promises and the quality targets ([[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]]).
questions.recommendation: Confirm the twenty-four as the base. If a way of growing you plan is missing, name it now, before the panel's brief is written: the panel designs against the cases it is given, and a case added later reaches the design rounds but not the panel's first proposals.

questions.title: Four readings of earlier decisions, to confirm
questions.decides: Whether four earlier decisions are read as overtaken by later ones, as the decision record reads them. The record keeps each earlier decision as made and flags the reading; nothing inferred is written as if you had said it.
evidence: [[dec:one-program-design-half-then-build-half]] had each build area start with its proof test failing on today's engine. Read as overtaken by [[dec:build-the-test-rig-when-building-starts]], which builds the rig as part of the new test bench where a thin first version of the new design runs end to end; the failing-test start returns only if the move from today's engine chooses to change it in place.

[[dec:the-nine-questions-the-pass-answers]], [[dec:five-documents-the-design-half-hands-over]] and [[dec:when-the-design-half-is-finished]] had one design choice per question, with the four questions on the game's live facts designed together. Read as overtaken by [[dec:design-top-down-hardest-to-reverse-choices-first]], which orders the design rounds by the hardest decisions to reverse, not by question. The record's reading is that the nine questions become checks on every design.

[[dec:five-documents-the-design-half-hands-over]] had proposals for the written lists of messages between the engine and the devices, drafted before code, as the third document the design half hands over. Read as overtaken by [[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]: one published, versioned protocol in place of today's scattered message lists and file formats.

[[dec:when-the-design-half-is-finished]] had the rig reproduce each finding marked for live proof before the design half ends. Read as overtaken by [[dec:build-the-test-rig-when-building-starts]], which moves the rig after design.
Each reading is flagged in its decision's entry under Decided, by topic, below.

options.label: Confirm all four readings.
options.cost: Four entries in the decision record are amended, and the design half's hand-over and end conditions are restated to match the top-down order.

options.label: Keep one or more of the earlier decisions as made.
options.cost: The design rounds then also write one design choice per question; each build area starts with its proof test failing on today's engine; proposals for the written lists of messages between the engine and the devices are drafted beside the protocol; and the rig reproduces each finding marked for live proof before the design half ends.

questions.recommendation: Confirm all four. The later decisions set the order the design half now follows; the earlier wordings stay in the record's history, and the nine questions keep their work as checks on every design.

questions.title: Are these the right ten promises?
questions.decides: Whether the ten promises on [[page:requirements]] are the base the pass designs for, with these titles, or something is missing, doubled or wrongly put; and whether each reads from the side of the people who count on it. This holds the earlier question "Is the list of design flaws right?".
evidence: Each promise says who counts on it, when, and what must happen for them. Every title is new; the earlier wording of each is in the [[page:changes]].
Every quality target and every extension case names the promises it serves; every promise is served by at least four targets and three cases.
The panel designs against the promises with your answers, so it runs only after you confirm them ([[dec:what-the-architects-panel-sees-and-when]]).
Whether running in any setup needs an eleventh promise is [[q:I]].
The earlier candidate on [[page:design]] names, for each promise, the parts that would keep it; every promise is kept by parts of its own.
On [[page:today]], each design flaw mainly breaks exactly one promise. No flaw mainly breaks [[promise:J6]] today; [[flaw:C8]] and [[flaw:C12]] break it beside others.
questions.recommendation: Keep these ten as the base, with these titles, and settle [[q:H]] to [[q:K]] below. In the earlier candidate every promise is kept by parts of its own, and the one candidate for an eleventh, "run in any setup", owns no part ([[q:I]]).

questions.title: Two clauses added to the pack promise
questions.decides: Whether both clauses added to "[[promise:J1]]" stay: that a second designer's game runs on the same engine, and that every device plays the same version of the pack and shows which.
evidence: The requirements ask for both. A designer who did not build ALN makes a whole second game, and that night the whole kit plays it, every tablet and scanner holding the same copy and the GM able to see that they match ([[ex:EX1]]); the engine holds none of ALN's words ([[qt:QT20]]); a pack change reaches every device with no restart, and the GM sees which version each device runs ([[qt:QT9]], [[ex:EX2]]).

In the earlier candidate, "Nothing in the engine assumes ALN" is a quality every part must have, named Generic on [[page:design]]. It is carried by [[part:P1]], which takes rules only from the pack, and by [[part:P12]] and [[part:P13]], which take the names of the kit's equipment only from the venue profile and from each running copy of the engine's own settings.
The version every device shows is the version mark [[part:P2]] puts on every copy and every game record, compared whenever a device connects.
A second designer's game on the same engine rests on the same part, [[part:P1]], which only calculates and changes nothing.
Today a tablet running a different pack than the engine is only written to a log, and nothing tells the GM ([[flaw:C12]]).
questions.recommendation: Keep both. The first is what lets other games run; the second is what the design flaw [[flaw:C12]] breaks.

questions.title: The roles promise covers who may act
questions.decides: Whether "[[promise:J7]]" keeps its second half: starting, pausing and ending the game, show control and score changes stay with staff who log in, such as the GM, and the stored passwords and keys change before outsiders touch the system.
evidence: The requirements say the same. A connection with no password or pass gets nothing, a read-only display pass cannot pause the game, only staff who log in can start, pause, end or reset a game, run show control or change a score, and the committed secrets rotate before the first outside designer sits down with the tool ([[qt:QT31]]). A designer may give a device class rights per game, but never past that limit ([[ex:EX11]]).
In the earlier candidate, one part, [[part:P7]], holds both each device's pass and what it allows, and [[part:P4]] checks the rule once, at the one place every request passes through.
The same rule is a quality every part must have, named "Only the GM moves the game" on [[page:design]].
Today a connection's own word decides what it gets: anyone on the kit network can fetch the whole game state, and the TV connects as if it were a GM tablet ([[flaw:C13]]).

questions.title: The venue promise names declared standalone
questions.decides: Whether the clause in "[[promise:J8]]" stays, that a standalone game is a choice the game declares and never mixed; and whether "[[flaw:N1]]" is a design flaw of its own, with its own design choice.
evidence: These are the words of your decision [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]] (2026-10-31): a whole game can run with no engine, as a choice a game declares, and no game mixes networked and standalone devices.

The requirements carry it: a declared standalone game in which every device says standalone and nothing shows red for the missing engine ([[qt:QT37]]); a mix refused with a reason ([[qt:QT38]]); a small game in a room with no show machine ([[ex:EX12]]).

The earlier candidate supports the clause: whether a game is standalone is something every design choice must take into account (the quality "Who decides when there is no engine"), and it is declared where the game is fitted to tonight's setup, under [[promise:J8]].

Where the declaration is kept is a choice for the design rounds: the venue profile, the pack, the game's record or each device. The earlier candidate favours the profile, because a profile that lists no engine equipment already makes every service the engine runs (video, music, lights) read "not installed tonight". Whichever is chosen, [[part:P2]] carries the declaration to every device.
Today the declaration is each tablet's own tap, the phone's web address and nothing on the hardware scanner; the pack has no field for it ([[flaw:N1]]).

The proposed flaw "[[flaw:N1]]" holds eight findings from the review of standalone games. If it is not a flaw of its own, they join [[flaw:C9]], [[flaw:C11]] and [[flaw:C14]] and the table comparing the hardware scanner with the phone's scanner. In the earlier candidate it is fixed in [[part:P2]] and [[part:P12]], or in [[part:P3]] if the declaration is kept there; your answer on the second point does not move it.
questions.recommendation: Agree. On the second point, yes: three other design choices (what each fact does between games, one answer per question, how old a copy is) need the declared fact as an input, and would otherwise each invent their own answer.

questions.title: Split the tap promise in two?
questions.decides: Whether the tap's answer and the night's record, the two halves of "[[promise:J3]]", are one promise or two. The parts are the same either way.
evidence: The night's record half names the director who tells the night's story and the players it is told to, beside you and the designer ([[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]], 2026-11-01).

The requirements already test the two halves at two moments: the tap's answer at the tap ([[qt:QT4]], [[qt:QT7]]); the night's record when the game ends ([[qt:QT16]]) and when the director reads it afterwards ([[ex:EX19]]).

Answering happens at the tap, for the GM or the player. The night's record is for after the show: what is captured during play, the record written when the game ends, the review. The earlier candidate confirms the two share no part: [[part:P4]] sits in the middle of the engine, and five promises depend on it; [[part:P5]] is written once, at the end of a game, and read afterwards.

[[part:P5]] carries the game the night ran and the texts the players saw (the same decision). The designer's Review reads it inside the engine; the game's own telling, for ALN the Director Console, reads it from outside, with room to run inside the Review stage later.

The tap's answer is mainly broken by [[flaw:C7]]: a reply never says which request it answers, or whether the answer is final or the scan was saved to send later. No design flaw mainly breaks the night's record half yet.
The alternatives table on [[page:design#alt-answer-and-record]] has this row: the tap's answer and the night's record, one part or two.

options.label: Keep one promise.
options.cost: The GM at the tap and the people after the show (the director, the players, you and the designer) look for what they count on in one sentence.

options.label: Split into two promises.
options.cost: Makes a promise that no design flaw mainly breaks yet, because the night's record is mostly planned work.

questions.recommendation: Split, into "Every tap gets its answer" and "The night can be told afterwards". The two halves serve different people at two moments and share no part, so two sentences let each find theirs.

questions.title: Keep the venue promise whole?
questions.decides: Whether running in any setup (no engine, another kit) gets a promise of its own, and which title the one promise carries if "[[promise:J8]]" stays one.
evidence: The requirements put all of it under the venue: a second production sets up a kit with a new profile and the same engine code ([[qt:QT24]], [[ex:EX16]]); a declared standalone game ([[qt:QT37]], [[ex:EX12]]); the venue technician's one preflight ([[qt:QT13]], [[ex:EX13]]).

Fitting the game to tonight's venue is one part with an output of its own: [[part:P12]] holds the venue technician's profile, which says what the kit brings, binds each of the pack's names to a real instrument and says whether the engine starts each program; [[part:P10]] turns it into one go or no-go.

Mapping how the promises fit together found that "run in any setup" has no part of its own. Running with no engine is a switch every design choice takes, declared as part of fitting the game. Running on another kit is each running copy of the engine keeping its own files, network ports and settings, [[part:P13]], the same part that keeps a test from touching the live show. A separate promise for it would own nothing.
The promise already names the venue technician, a GM running a game with no engine and a future operator with a second kit.

This promise is mainly broken by "[[flaw:N1]]". [[flaw:C15]] also breaks it: program names and install commands are fixed to one operating-system release, so a new machine logs warnings or refuses its install.
The earlier recommendation, to split, is in the [[page:changes#rec-e]].

options.label: Split: a promise of its own for running in any setup.
options.cost: It would own no part.

options.label: One promise, titled "The game fits the venue, whatever the setup".
options.cost: Keeps standalone games and other kits in the title; the venue technician's moment moves to the sentences.

options.label: One promise, titled "The game fits the venue it is in tonight".
options.cost: Names the venue technician's moment; the GM running a standalone game and a future operator with another kit are named in a sentence, not in a title.

questions.recommendation: One promise, titled "The game fits the venue it is in tonight", with standalone games kept in its first sentences.

questions.title: Proof and release in one promise?
questions.decides: Whether the developer's tests, which show a change to the engine works before it reaches a show, and your release day stay in one promise, "[[promise:J10]]", split, move release day under the venue technician, or go back to a sentence about tests alone. This holds the earlier question "Flaws none of the pass's questions covers".
evidence: The requirements test the two moments apart. Every change runs the full set of tests twice, once with ALN's pack and once with the toy game's, and a skipped test never counts as a pass ([[qt:QT26]]). On release day the show machine carries one written list of what it should hold, and rolling back moves every piece ([[qt:QT41]], [[ex:EX17]]).
You have since decided that the tests become a test bench outside the engine, with Proof kept as a quality every part must meet ([[dec:one-published-protocol-and-an-outside-test-bench]]).

The earlier candidate separates this promise's two moments. Before every change, the developer's tests pass and show the show still works for ALN and for the toy game, the small second game kept for tests; that is a quality every part must have (Proof, on [[page:design]]), and checking that parts which pass things to each other agree is part of it. [[part:P16]] and [[part:P13]] carry it.

On release day, you decide when a new version goes to the venue and can swap back by replugging a machine. That is one small part, [[part:P17]]: what is installed is one written list of what the machine should carry, which the engine compares at start, so a rollback moves everything or says what it did not.

Four flaws mainly break this promise. The pass's question "Only the live engine touches the show" covers keeping tests away from it ([[flaw:C8]]). For the other three none of the nine questions fits: "One question gets one answer" is only the nearest for the names two parts share ([[flaw:C14]]), and the installed pieces ([[flaw:C15]]) and tests that prove the real path ([[flaw:C16]]) have none ([[dec:the-nine-questions-the-pass-answers]]).
Every option below gives [[flaw:C15]] a part to be fixed in; [[flaw:C16]] is fixed in [[part:P16]] whichever you choose.

The alternatives table on [[page:design#alt-release]] has this row: release day as its own part beside the developer's tests, or in [[part:P12]]'s hand-off from designer to venue technician to GM. The earlier recommendation is in the [[page:changes#rec-f]].

options.label: a. Keep one promise covering both moments, as the title does.
options.cost: One title covers two people at two moments, the developer's tests and your release day; the recommendation gives each a question of its own among the pass's questions.

options.label: b. Split release day into a promise of its own.
options.cost: It gives your release day its own sentence, kept by one small part.

options.label: c. File release day with the venue technician's set-up work, under "[[promise:J8]]".
options.cost: The check of what is installed sits where the venue technician works, but your decision to send a version moves away from the developer's tests.

options.label: d. Go back to the earlier wording, about tests alone.
options.cost: The parts fit that too; the cost is that your release day stays unnamed.

questions.recommendation: One promise, as the title has it, and give the developer's tests and your release day a question each among the pass's questions, which would serve as checks on every design if you confirm [[q:C]]. Both moments exist so that nothing reaches the live show unproven, or before you say so.

questions.title: Which promise carries equipment state on screens?
questions.decides: Whether the route that carries the equipment's state to the screens is named in "[[promise:J4]]", in "[[promise:J2]]", or in neither.
evidence: The requirements name the need without naming a promise: when the engine is killed, no screen anywhere shows a calm, current-looking value for a fact it cannot confirm ([[qt:QT5]]); for any fact a screen shows, one place decides it and every screen traces to it ([[qt:QT17]]). The pass's question "Service state travels with its health" asks the same ([[dec:the-nine-questions-the-pass-answers]]).

If the design rounds keep one delivery part, neither promise needs to name the route: in the earlier candidate [[part:P6]] carries every fact to every screen, game facts and equipment alike, each with its label (how sure, how old); six promises use it.
[[part:P8]] decides each program's state and health as one dated fact; [[part:P6]] carries it; [[part:P14]] draw it.

The two promises already cover their halves. Under [[promise:J4]], the GM makes the room do a thing and sees it happen, or sees at once that it did not. Under [[promise:J2]], every screen agrees, also after a tablet comes back. The game's running state there already includes the video queue, music, held items, the clock and each service's health.
This question places [[flaw:C2]], where today health and state travel on separate routes, so the music card keeps its playing look while the health row turns red.

The design rounds choose between one delivery part and the parts behind each promise delivering their own facts; the alternatives table on [[page:design#alt-delivery]] has that row. The earlier answer is in the [[page:changes#rec-g]].

options.label: Name the route in neither promise.
options.cost: Holds only as long as the design rounds keep one delivery part.

options.label: Name it under "[[promise:J4]]".
options.cost: The words sit with the equipment whose state it is, but that promise then names a route the other also needs.

options.label: Name it under "[[promise:J2]]".
options.cost: The words match how the game's running state is already defined, but that promise then carries the equipment beside the game's record.

questions.recommendation: Add the route to neither promise, as long as the design rounds keep one delivery part; both then hold through it, and the card for [[flaw:C2]] stays under "[[promise:J4]]", where its moment at a show is felt. If the design rounds choose the other way, with the parts behind each promise delivering their own facts, the route belongs with the room promise, beside that card.

questions.title: The hardware scanner's standalone mode
questions.decides: Whether the hardware scanner gets a standalone mode to match the phone's scanner, as parity work the pass must serve. Your explicit word is asked for.
evidence: [[dec:standalone-games-declared-never-mixed]] (2026-10-31) recorded the hardware scanner's missing standalone mode as a parity gap, not a new feature, because the two player scanners keep feature parity wherever possible.

The requirements already read it that way: the hardware scanner plays a standalone game as the phone's scanner does, and its missing standalone mode is closed as a parity gap ([[qt:QT39]]); the phone's scanner and the hardware scanner drive the same pack-declared actions ([[qt:QT22]], [[ex:EX10]]).
The table comparing the hardware scanner with the phone's scanner, on [[page:today#standalone]], compares 24 abilities; with no engine the hardware scanner trails the phone in seven of them.
Today the hardware scanner treats a missing engine as an outage that never ends: a red Disconnected, a growing queue, and "Rescan later" for a video that can never play ([[flaw:C10]], [[flaw:N1]]).
In the earlier candidate [[part:P2]] carries the declaration to every device with its pack.

options.label: Yes.
options.cost: The standalone declaration must reach a device that has no idea of it today.

options.label: No.
options.cost: Leaves the hardware scanner behind the phone with no engine, in seven of the 24 abilities the table compares, and showing a missing engine as a red outage all night.

questions.recommendation: Yes, as your parity rule asks.

questions.title: One GM tablet per standalone game?
questions.decides: Whether one tablet decides everything in a standalone game, and whether a standalone tablet's record of the night can hold player scans.
evidence: The requirements leave the count to you: [[ex:EX12]] carries the number of GM tablets one standalone game may run as a number to set; [[qt:QT37]] names the count open, and [[qt:QT39]] names the second point open: whether a standalone game's record holds what the players found.
Today two standalone tablets are two separate games: each holds its own claim list, so one token can be sold on both, and each holds its own score table ([[flaw:C1]]).
A standalone tablet's record of the night ([[part:P5]]) can hold player scans only if the standalone player scanners hand their scans to that tablet.
Player devices need to learn each new game: a game id from the tablet that they check, if they are joined to it, or a reset of their own ([[flaw:C4]]).

In the earlier candidate the tablet runs the engine's [[part:P3]] and [[part:P11]], or an engine of its own kept equal by tests; the alternatives table on [[page:design#alt-standalone-tablet]] has that row.

options.label: One tablet.
options.cost: Standalone games with two GMs are ruled out.

options.label: Several tablets sharing one game.
options.cost: They would need to talk to each other directly, a large new piece.

questions.recommendation: One tablet, unless you plan standalone games with two GMs.

questions.title: Exposed evidence and video with no engine
questions.decides: What the screens draw in two cases in a game with no engine and no TV: a token exposed as evidence, and a video token.
evidence: The requirements name both open: how exposure and video tokens behave with no engine ([[qt:QT39]], [[ex:EX12]]).

In detective-style modes the pack says an exposure shows on the scoreboard. On a tablet alone the scoreboard screen shows only modes that rank teams (like Black Market) and the list that picks which evidence to show is hidden, so the GM sees the summary once, on the result screen, and "exposed means public" has no standalone effect ([[flaw:N1]]).
A video token on the phone shows a black screen with the token's id; on the hardware scanner, its picture and "Rescan later", which never works ([[flaw:N1]], [[flaw:C10]]).

The screens that would draw either answer are [[part:P14]]; in the earlier candidate a small [[part:P10]] stand-in on the tablet marks every service the engine runs "not installed tonight": grey, never red.
The review of standalone games left both answers to you: what a video token shows with no engine is a declared answer standalone needs, not a fault to fix.

options.label: Exposed evidence on the tablet's own scoreboard screen; a video token shows its picture with a plain note.
options.cost: Needs the tablet's own scoreboard screen to show exposed evidence.

options.label: Show nothing for exposure and hide video tokens.
options.cost: Smaller, but drops a mode's effect from a standalone game.

questions.recommendation: Exposed evidence shows on the GM tablet's own scoreboard screen, which standalone already has. A video token shows its picture with a plain note instead of an error.

questions.title: Record every refused GM scan attempt?
questions.decides: Whether the game's record keeps refused attempts (a token already used, or no game running), or only the answer goes back to the tablet.
evidence: The requirements say the result screen never says complete for a refused scan and shows the engine's reason ([[qt:QT7]]), and that the night's record carries what was sold and exposed, by whom and when ([[qt:QT16]]); neither says whether a refused attempt is kept.
Today a refused GM scan is told to the tablet that scanned and recorded nowhere else. The review that named the design flaws set this aside as a product choice no design flaw decides.
In the earlier candidate [[part:P3]] is where the game's facts are decided and the answer goes back through [[part:P4]].
Where [[promise:J3]] lists [[flaw:C9]] among its flaws, it leaves this to you: whether refused scans belong in the night's record is your open question, not that flaw's.
A standalone tablet records refused duplicates and unknown tokens nowhere either; a yes needs a standalone counterpart, which the change for [[flaw:C7]] carries.

options.label: Yes.
options.cost: The record gains a kind of fact that no screen shows yet.

options.label: No.
options.cost: Nothing is recorded, as today, and the night's record cannot tell a refused attempt.

questions.recommendation: Yes. Record every attempt and its answer, and show it nowhere until a feature needs it.

designRounds.text: How the engine holds the game's state: the facts of a running game that can change during it, where each is kept, and how every screen's copy of them stays true.

The published protocol's form: the protocol itself is decided; this round settles how each message and each file that crosses the engine's edge (what a device may ask, what the engine answers, what it tells screens, and the files that carry a game or a night) is defined and versioned.
Where authority lives across devices, offline and standalone included: which place decides each fact when a tablet is disconnected, and when a game runs with no engine at all.
How games and venues extend the engine: what a pack and a venue profile can declare, and where a developer adds support for a device, a program, a scoring model or a content source.

How one engine runs as many separate copies: the show's copy, a trial copy and a test run on one machine, each keeping its own files, network ports and settings, and a second kit on another machine. Where the designer's trial copy runs, a laptop or the show machine between games, is open.

How today's engine moves to the new design: the build plan starts with a thin first version of the new design on the new test bench; whether today's engine is instead changed in place is part of this decision.

later.text: Where "this game is standalone" is declared: the venue profile (the earlier candidate favours it), the pack, the game's record or each device. It falls inside the round on where authority lives.
Getting facts onto screens: one delivery part for every fact, or the parts behind each promise delivering their own facts in one shared format.
The life of a game: one lifecycle part that alone moves the game and resets every part, or a table each part reads and applies itself.
The game rules as one shared body of code that the engine and the tablet both run, or two bodies kept equal by tests.
The equipment's interface: one per kind of thing the room can do (play a video, light a scene), or one per outside program.
The standalone tablet: the same record and lifecycle parts the engine runs, or an engine of its own.
The scoreboard: one page in two places, or a view inside the GM app.
The config tool: a separate program that talks to the engine only by sending it requests, never by writing its files, or pages the engine itself serves.
When a new version of the game may be loaded while the engine runs. That is not built yet; the plan allows it only before a game starts or after it ends.

Where the setting lives that says whether the engine starts each outside program or uses one already running: in the venue technician's profile, as the earlier candidate has it, or in a file of its own, as the list of planned capabilities you approved has it.

The order of the build half's work, for the build plan: by part, with [[part:P13]] (each running copy of the engine keeping its own files, network ports and settings) and [[part:P6]] first since most flaws fall to them, or by the roadmap's blocks, each by its name.

Whether paper documents join the pack, with "unlocked" recorded during play, so the night's record can say which documents the players opened. [[dec:the-night-s-record-and-the-after-game-article]] left this to the design rounds; today the director marks them by hand after the show.

entries.title: Design for the long term, beyond ALN
entries.line: The pass designs the best architecture for the engine's next iteration, for long-term use as it grows beyond ALN; the fixes and findings from blue, the show machine in use now, are clues to where today's design is off, never the driver.

entries.title: The architecture pass is the work now
entries.line: The pass is the current work, design half first, and covers the whole engine: the engine's server, the GM scanner, the two player scanners, the scoreboards and the config tool; blue keeps running the game until the new engine is ready to swap in on green, the second show machine being built, and no date governs the work.

entries.title: Blue's fixes are evidence of design causes
entries.line: Blue's fixes and unfixed findings are evidence of where today's design is weak, never the driver; fixes that share a cause become one design decision, and the sixteen design flaws are test situations every design is checked against.

entries.title: Four words for the game's live facts
entries.line: Runtime state (every fact about a running game that can change during it), authority (the place that decides a fact), copy (that fact held anywhere else) and delivery path (its route from the authority to a screen) are in the glossary; an outside program can be an authority.

entries.title: Promises, qualities, moments, venue technician
entries.line: A promise is what a person can count on at a given moment; a quality is something every part must have so a promise holds everywhere; a moment is when a promise matters; the person who fits a kit to a venue is the venue technician; promises carry titles only.

entries.title: Name each step by what it does
entries.line: The pass has a design half and a build half; its steps are the requirements, the panel, the design rounds, the build plan, the hostile review, the final questions and your sign-off; blocks go by name, question rounds by date and test levels by name.

entries.title: The nine questions the pass answers
entries.line: The pass answers nine questions for the whole engine, from who decides each fact to whether a reconnecting screen's catch-up is built like its live update; the nine stand, and since the design went top-down they are read as checks on each design ([[q:C]]).

entries.title: The role question starts from settled roles
entries.line: The components keep their settled roles: the player scanners show token content and report scans, with no scoring; the GM scanner is the command center; the scoreboards show the public results; the question on roles starts from these.

entries.title: Standalone games: declared, never mixed
entries.line: A whole game can run with no engine, as a choice a game declares; no game mixes networked and standalone devices; standalone games join the list every design choice must serve. The hardware scanner's missing standalone mode is a parity gap, pending your word ([[q:L]]).

entries.title: The night's record and the after-game article
entries.line: What the players receive after the show is the game's business, outside the engine; the second half of the promise [[promise:J3]], that the night can be told afterwards, names the director and the players after the show; the night's record carries the pack the game ran and the texts the players saw; players' emails stay outside the engine; the Director Console stays a separate program that reads the record; the two clocks (a sale stamped with the tablet's time, an adjustment with the engine computer's) join [[flaw:C9]].

entries.title: One published protocol and an outside test bench
entries.line: One published, versioned protocol defines everything that crosses the engine's edge, the files that carry a game or a night included, and is designed in an early design round; the tests become a test bench outside the engine, with Proof kept as a quality. Together they replace the earlier candidate's part [[part:P16]].

decided.topic: How the design is made, and in what order

entries.title: One program: design half, then build half
entries.line: The design half decides the shared design choices with you, one question round at a time, and ends with the new roadmap; the build half changes the engine one area at a time, starting with a thin first version on a new test bench. Whether each area starts with its test failing on today's engine is [[q:C]].

entries.title: Run the pass like the re-charter
entries.line: The pass is a roadmap revision run the way the September re-charter ran: evidence, a draft with questions, a hostile review, question rounds, your sign-off; its roadmap becomes the roadmap's next revision, and on your pages the questions go by title.

entries.title: The truth sweep's charter is retired
entries.line: The truth sweep's charter is retired; its purpose, proving that every screen tells the truth, moves into the build work the pass plans, and its census and five recorded desync bugs are evidence for the pass.

entries.title: Five documents the design half hands over
entries.line: The design half hands over the design choices, one per question, with proof tests in plain words, the review that named the design flaws with every fix and finding assigned or set aside, proposals for the written lists of messages between the engine and the devices, one decision note per hard-to-reverse choice, and the new roadmap; two parts are read as overtaken ([[q:C]]).

entries.title: The design half's method and tools
entries.line: The design half's order is the review that named the design flaws (done), the requirements, the panel, the design rounds, the build plan, the hostile review, the final questions and your sign-off; each round writes two or three designs side by side, published as pages for you and checked against the promises, the quality targets, the extension cases and the sixteen design flaws.

entries.title: When the design half is finished
entries.line: The design half ends at your sign-off once every finding and blue fix is assigned or set aside with a reason, every design choice says how it serves the planned capabilities and standalone games, the hostile review's blocking findings are resolved, every question has its design choice and proof test, and the rig reproduces each finding marked for live proof; the last two conditions are read as overtaken ([[q:C]]).

entries.title: Corrections to the readers and the hardening pieces
entries.line: The merged hardening pieces (the equipment families, the core that marks equipment not installed tonight, the harness minimum) stay in the engine and change only where a design choice requires; the review's readers were split by source, merged by cause and checked, and that work is done.

entries.title: Build the test rig when building starts
entries.line: The test rig is built at the start of building, as part of the new test bench where a thin first version of the new design runs end to end, not before design; the exception is a move that changes today's engine in place. The question on how much the rig proves before design is withdrawn.

entries.title: Design top-down, hardest-to-reverse choices first
entries.line: The rest of the design half goes top-down: finish the requirements, then design rounds ordered by the hardest decisions to reverse (the six under Coming in the design rounds), each with two or three designs checked against the requirements and the sixteen design flaws, then a build plan that starts with a thin first version; this site is reframed to the long-term frame.

entries.title: Independent architects propose the top-level design
entries.line: An independent panel of architects, who have not seen the reasoning of the orchestrator (the agent running the pass), proposes and stress-tests the top-level design decisions before the first design round; its brief comes to you first.

entries.title: What the architects' panel sees, and when
entries.line: The panel first gets the goal, the requirements and the setting; only after its first proposals does it get today's engine as facts and the sixteen design flaws as test situations; withheld are the orchestrator's recommendations, the earlier candidate (it enters a second round as one more proposal) and the earlier lists of design choices. It runs after you confirm the requirements.

entries.title: The owner's site: five linked pages
entries.line: Your page is linked pages built from one set of data, with a change log for earlier wordings; the same decision asks for the long-term frame and for titles in place of numbers, which this version applies, regrouping the pages as the engine, decisions, requirements, design, today's engine and the change log.

entries.title: Green's follow-ups ship when the definition session ends
entries.line: Green's three follow-ups (a false boot warning on a correct green, the second show machine being built, two lines missing from the environment template, an install instruction the new operating system refuses) shipped as one small task when the definition session ended; merged 2026-10-30.

entries.title: Decide in question rounds, never at sign-off
entries.line: Every decision is made in a question round with the evidence in view and written into its document at once; documents record decisions and never make them; anything new found while writing comes back to you as a question; your sign-off is a skim with no new decisions.

entries.title: The owner ratified the program document
entries.line: You ratified the program document, the plan for this review, on 2026-10-30; the definition session closed and the pass became the current work, design half first.

entries.title: No rule for documents: fix as we go
entries.line: The pass has no rule for written documents (guides, READMEs, contracts, code comments) that disagree with the code; they are fixed as we go, by the same piece of work that finds the disagreement; dated records stay as written.

entries.title: Titles, not numbers, and a topic record
entries.line: Decisions, questions and design flaws go by short plain titles in conversation and on your pages, ids stay inside records, and the decision record is reorganized by topic, each decision written as current truth with a dated history beneath.
